answer.Body: Both indices are measures of strength of association (i.e. whether any predictor is associated with the outcome, as for an LR test), and can be used to quantify predictive ability or model performance. A single predictor may have a significant effect on the outcome but it might not necessarily be so useful for predicting individual response, hence the need to assess model performance as a whole (wrt. the null model). The Nagelkerke $R^2$ is useful because it has a maximum value of 1.0, as Srikant said. This is just a normalized version of the $R^2$ computed from the likelihood ratio, $R^2_{\text{LR}}=1-\exp(-\text{LR}/n)$, which has connection with the Wald statistic for overall association, as originally proposed by Cox and Snell. | Other indices of predictive ability are Brier score, the C index (concordance probability or ROC area), or Somers' D, the latter two providing a better measure of predictive discrimination.
